analysis.one_liner: Requires new cars to average 33 mpg by 2017 and lets automakers trade fuel-economy credits.
analysis.headline: No action was taken beyond an initial committee referral in the 109th Congress; the bill had no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Transportation Department to write fuel economy rules guaranteeing that cars built after 2016 average at least 33 miles per gallon, up from the low-to-mid-20s standard then in place. It also created a credit-trading program so automakers that beat the standard could sell credits to those that fell short, and allowed different standards for different vehicle sizes. The bill was introduced in June 2006 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers would benefit from significantly lower gasoline costs, since the bill would roughly double the fleet average fuel economy of new cars over a decade. Reduced gasoline consumption would also cut household exposure to volatile fuel prices and reduce pollution.

how_it_helps.text: Requires average new-car fuel economy to reach at least 33 mpg for vehicles made after 2016.
Directs the Secretary of Transportation to set escalating standards beginning with model years after 2008 to reach that 33 mpg target.
Requires that efficiency improvements not degrade vehicle safety, addressing a common objection to higher fuel economy mandates.
Creates a credit-trading program so manufacturers that exceed the standards can sell credits to those that fall short, lowering overall compliance costs.
Allows separate standards for different vehicle-size classes.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, especially those selling larger, less efficient vehicles, would bear the engineering and compliance costs of meeting higher fuel economy standards. Gasoline refiners would see reduced demand over time. Some of the compliance cost could be passed to new-car buyers in the short run, though it would be offset by lower fuel spending over the life of the vehicle.

drawbacks.text: Higher upfront new-vehicle costs could fall hardest on buyers of large vehicles or those who need them for work, even accounting for fuel savings.

The bill leaves details largely to the Transportation Department rather than setting specific interim-year standards, giving an administration wide latitude over how quickly the 33 mpg target is actually reached.
Credit trading could allow some manufacturers to keep selling very inefficient vehicles as long as others overcomply, concentrating the real-world efficiency gains unevenly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit to households is substantial: fuel costs are a large recurring expense and a mandate to reach 33 mpg would meaningfully cut them over time. The costs fall on manufacturers and are partly offset by fuel savings for buyers. The main design weakness is flexibility: the bill sets an endpoint but delegates the pace and detail to regulators, which could weaken the guarantee depending on who holds the office.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it died without any further action before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on June 7, 2006.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On June 23, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality.
No further action was taken, and the bill had no cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers—particularly those whose fleets relied on large, low-mileage vehicles—avoided a binding 33 mpg requirement, and the subcommittee process ensured the bill never advanced. Drivers did not get the lower fuel costs the bill would have provided, though Congress later raised fuel economy standards through other legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with no cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would impose compliance costs on automakers, especially those selling large, inefficient vehicles, but the credit-trading program lowers the cost of meeting the target and rewards overcompliance. Drivers, not the industry, would capture most of the benefit through lower fuel spending.
Higher vehicle efficiency reduces gasoline consumption, cutting long-run demand for the industry's product. Cheaper fuel bills for drivers are the flip side of lower refiner revenue.
